title: The Compendium of Super-Quadratic Computational Quantum Advantages
authors: Philipp Kammerlander, Thomas E. O'Brien, Robbie King, Rolando D. Somma, Mária Kieferová, Brad Lackey, Alexander Schmidhuber, Siddhartha Jain, Andi Gu, Yuri Alexeev, Shouvanik Chakrabarti, Ruslan Shaydulin, Pietro M. Posta, Guang Hao Low, Dar Gilboa, Matthias Troyer, Barry C. Sanders, Matthias Christandl, Elica Kyoseva, Catherine Lefebvre, Ryan Babbush
abstract: This compendium presents a structured collection of computational problems with credible prospects for realizing meaningful quantum advantage, focused on describing problem characteristics rather than specific algorithms. It is intended for non-quantum researchers and practitioners with strong computational backgrounds, particularly domain experts, seeking to assess the relevance of quantum methods to real-world problems. The compendium focuses on enumerating core problems for which there is good evidence that a quantum computer can realize more than a quadratic speedup in offline non-relativized time-complexity (e.g., as opposed to in oracular settings, streaming models, or communication advantages). Entries characterize the structural constraints that real-world instances must satisfy to realize those advantages in practice. The intention is to provide a reference that can be leveraged to connect quantum algorithms to practical use cases.
summary: This paper compiles a reference guide detailing computational problems that are theoretically expected to yield super-quadratic quantum speedups. It moves beyond abstract algorithms by focusing on the structural properties of real-world problems that can harness this advantage. This framework is designed to bridge the gap between quantum complexity theory and practical domain expertise.
main_problem: To provide a structured, accessible compendium of computational problems that show credible prospects for achieving super-quadratic quantum speedups over classical methods.
main_result: The paper establishes a framework (Stages I, II, III) to guide researchers in connecting theoretical quantum advantage primitives to practical, real-world computational use cases.
method: It analyzes the structural constraints required for a problem family to yield a super-quadratic speedup, focusing on problem characterization rather than specific algorithms.
model_or_system: The focus is on abstract computational problems (families of instances) rather than a specific physical Hamiltonian or quantum hardware platform. It distinguishes between problem structure and algorithmic implementation.
key_observables: Super-quadratic speedup in offline non-relativized time-complexity.
important_parameters: The required structural constraints on real-world instances to guarantee the asymptotic advantage.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a solid computational background for the reader and acknowledges that I/O and data movement costs can negate theoretical speedups.
paper_structure: The content is structured into 'Stage I Problems: Primitives with Evidence for Quantum Advantage' and 'Stage II Problems: Concrete Instances Exhibiting Quantum Advantage,' guiding the transition toward practical application.
why_interesting: While highly theoretical, the rigorous classification of *where* quantum advantage might exist provides a crucial roadmap for applying quantum computation to complex physical simulations, especially those involving differential equations or topological invariants.
